Nothing in it was tried on new passages. Every number is read-only arithmetic on the old v1.2 label files. That arithmetic is practice, not a verdict. No project file was changed. HOW EVERY OLD DISAGREEMENT WAS SORTED. Four piles.
Pile 1, pointing: which words to copy. This study may fix that (rule 16).
Pile 2, a contradiction inside guide v1.2. Fixed by removing the contradiction, not by adding a meaning.
Pile 3, a question about what a definition covers, where guide v1.2 is silent or says two things. NOT decided. The entry is still written. It is marked `held`, counted in its own row, and the question goes to the owner.
Pile 4, a place where guide v1.2 already took a side in plain words. That side is kept and said plainly. It is still listed for the owner.
Part A stays word for word. Rule 15 is not edited. Rule 8 (no Worlds, Domains, Drives or Registers) stays. The owner's two open questions are not decided.

THE PASSAGE RECORD is unchanged: passage_id, none_of_these, entries, not_enough_information, guide_problem.

ONE ENTRY = one thing, in one role, for one Mind. Every quoted field is an exact copy from the passage, one unbroken stretch.
1. `noetic`: '^1' to '^9'.
2. `mind`: the `label` of this team's own `^1` entry for that Mind, character for character. Empty only for `^6`. In a `^1` entry, `mind` equals its own `label`.
3. `label`: the short identifying name of the thing. 1 to 12 words (stretches between spaces). It lies inside `support`. Never a naming phrase cut down to its bare noun.
4. `support`: the full supporting quote. Whole sentences, at most 4. It holds the label and, for `^4` and `^7`, the measure. It is where the meaning is kept. It is never compared between teams.
5. `measure`: only for `^4` (the how-much words) and `^7` (the rate and pattern words; in a held H7-RESULT entry the without-thinking words; in a held H7-UNBROKEN entry the unbroken word). It lies inside `support`. Empty for every other Noetic.
6. `relative_to`: `^8`: the label of its `^9`. `^9`: the label of its `^8` (empty only with `reached_by`). `^6`: the whole (empty only with `clue`). Empty for `^1`, `^2`, `^3`, `^4`, `^5`, `^7`.
7. `certainty`: 'clear', 'ambiguous' or 'held'.
8. `other_candidate`: only with ambiguous: '^n', 'none' or 'reasoning' (rule 15(d), unchanged).
9. `held_under`: only with held. One of 8 codes: H2-COMFORT, H3-NOPULL, H3-BORED, H5-ROLE, H7-RESULT, H7-NOEFFECT, H7-UNBROKEN, H89-FOLLOWS (rule 17).
10. `reached_by`: 'reasoning', only on a `^9` under rule 15(b). Unchanged.
11. `clue`: true, only on a `^6`, and only in a passage where this team wrote a `^9` with `reached_by` reasoning (rule 7).
12. `no_fuller_name`: true, optional. Only when no noun anywhere in the passage names the thing.

EXAMPLE. Made-up passage: 'Maren opened the old ledger. The dry smell of ink and dust rose from its pages. That smell put her back in her father's shop, counting coins into paper rolls.' Shown here with single quotes; the file uses JSON double quotes.

WHAT MOVED FROM v1.2. The field `words` is gone. For `^2`, `^3`, `^5`, `^6`, `^8`, `^9` it splits into `label` (short) and `support` (full). For `^4` and `^7` the old `words` (how-much words, rate words) becomes `measure`, and the old `relative_to` (the thing) becomes `label`. So every label names a thing, and nothing is lost.

WHAT CHANGED FROM THE DRAFT AFTER THE REVIEW (format and checker only; the rule changes are in the other sections).
- A dropped entry no longer vanishes. It stays in its row as an unmatched entry.
- A `^1` label is located at the first place the name occurs in the passage, whatever the support.
- `clue` is set by a mechanical rule, not by the labeler's judgment.
- The labeler does not write a `^5` on the label of its own `^7`. The program adds that `^5` itself and reports `^5` both ways.
- A label may have 12 words, not 10. My own check found a rule-following label with 11 words ('the familiar, sharp scent of salt spray and warm diesel fumes', V077).
- A support may have at most 4 sentences.
- H5-ROLE and H89-FOLLOWS are narrower. The other six codes keep their scope.
- The draft's step 'a thing and something of it' is deleted.

THE CHECKER. Plain Python, no model. One program, the same for both teams, frozen and hashed before labeling. It runs on one team's output for one passage. It never sees the other team's labels. A re-ask shows the passage, that team's own entry, the names of the failed checks and a fixed message. Up to three tries per passage, as in plan v1.2.
C1. Allowed values. `noetic` is '^1' to '^9'. `certainty` is clear, ambiguous or held. `other_candidate` is there only with ambiguous. `held_under` is there only with held and belongs to that Noetic. `reached_by` only on a `^9`. `clue` only on a `^6`, and only when this team's record for the passage has a `^9` with `reached_by` reasoning.
C2. `support` is an exact copy from the passage, after one fixed clean-up (curly quotes to straight quotes, runs of spaces to one space). The program then widens it to whole sentences. The widened support has at most 4 sentences.
C3. `label` is an exact copy, lies inside the widened support, and has 1 to 12 words. For `^1` the support must hold the name; the label is then located at the first place the name occurs in the passage, whatever the support.
C4. `measure` is filled and lies inside the support for `^4` and `^7`. It is empty for every other Noetic.
C5. `mind` equals the label of one of this team's own `^1` entries in the passage (empty only for `^6`).
C6. `relative_to`. `^8`: equals the label of a `^9` entry with the same mind, the same certainty and the same hold code, and that `^9` points back. `^9`: the reverse, or empty with `reached_by`. An entry may be written again with the same label when each copy points at a different partner (rule 16, step 10). `^6`: an exact copy from the passage of 1 to 12 words, or empty with `clue` true. All other Noetics: empty.
C7. Pointer check on every `label` except a `^1` label, and on a `^6` `relative_to`, unless `no_fuller_name` is true. Not a pronoun alone (it, this, that, they, them, he, she, here, there, one). Not starting with this, that, these, those or such. Not 'the', 'a' or 'an' plus one bare word from this fixed list: sound, noise, smell, scent, odour, odor, aroma, fragrance, sight, feeling, sensation, memory, image, picture, thought, moment. Not starting with a holder lead-in: 'a memory of', 'the memory of', 'memories of', 'a picture of', 'pictures of', 'an image of', 'a vision of', 'a thought of', 'the thought of'.
C8. No duplicate. No two entries of one team in one passage that the scorer's own test would call the same reading.
C9. One re-ask, never a rejection. For `^2` and `^3`: the last content word of the label is a feeling word (satisfaction, pleasure, comfort, peace, calm, relief, aversion, annoyance, disgust, unease, irritation, distaste, dislike, yearning, longing, feeling, sense). Fixed message: 'Your label names a feeling. If it is the Mind's own pull or push and the passage names what it is aimed at, use that thing as the label. If the feeling is itself what the Mind is drawn to or repelled by, send the same label again.' The second answer is accepted.
DROPS. An entry that still fails C1 to C8 after the third try is dropped. A dropped entry does not vanish. If its `noetic` and `certainty` are valid, it stays in its row as an unmatched entry of that team, with the reason DROPPED. It counts in that team's entries, in the cases and in the presence measure. It can never be matched. If its `noetic` or `certainty` is not valid, it cannot be put in a row; it is counted as 'dropped, no row'. More than 5% of a team's entries dropped (both kinds together) makes the verdict invalid (kept from plan v1.2). The report gives re-asks and drops per team, per check and per Noetic. Why: a reviewer showed on the old labels that dropping one side of a disagreement would move `^8` from 0.472 to 0.541 and `^9` from 0.478 to 0.533 while the verdict stayed valid.

spec.pointing_rule_exact_text:
This text replaces the `words`, `mind` and `relative_to` bullets under 'Rules for the fields', rule 12, and all of rule 16 of guide v1.2. Part A is not touched. Rule 15 is not touched.

16. **How to point: label, supporting quote, measure.** Every entry points at one thing: the Mind or the Idea that holds the Noetic. Do these steps in this order.

**Step 1. Find the evidence sentence.** It is the sentence whose words make the thing hold the role.
- `^1`: the sentence with the first full mention of the name.
- `^2`, `^3`: the first sentence that has a word of affinity, pull or aversion aimed at the thing, or that shows a move toward it or away from it.
- `^4`: the sentence with the how-much words.
- `^5`: the sentence that says what was lived or learned.
- `^6`: the sentence that lists the part.
- `^7`: the sentence with the rate or pattern words.
- `^8`, `^9`: the sentence with the bringing words (rule 2).
- A held kind (rule 17): the sentence with the words rule 17 names for that code: the good-feeling words (H2-COMFORT), the no-appeal words (H3-NOPULL), the boredom words (H3-BORED), the role words (H5-ROLE), the without-thinking words (H7-RESULT), the rate words (H7-NOEFFECT), the unbroken word (H7-UNBROKEN), the remembering words (H89-FOLLOWS).
If you find no such words and no held kind fits, write no entry.

**Step 2. Take the label from the evidence sentence.** The `label` is the naming of the thing in the evidence sentence, as the passage words it there. If that sentence names the thing more than once, take the first naming that is not a pointer (step 3). Do not swap it for an earlier, different naming: 'The dryer noise faded quickly in her awareness' gives 'The dryer noise', although an earlier sentence says 'A sudden metallic clanging from the industrial dryer'. Do not swap it for the thing it belongs to: 'feeling a pull towards its mechanical might' gives 'its mechanical might', not 'the heavy excavator'; the trigger is 'Its lanolin scent', not 'a roll of raw tweed'.
If the evidence sentence does not name the thing, or names it only with pointers, go to the nearest sentence that names it outright. For the thing brought to Mind (`^9`) look forward: first later in the same sentence, then in the next sentence. For everything else go back one sentence at a time. Take the naming of what the pointer points at. That need not be the first noun of that sentence: in 'The air filled with the familiar, sharp scent of salt spray and warm diesel fumes. It brought to his thoughts ...' the trigger is the scent, the thing noticed, not 'The air' that carries it. A describing phrase after 'was' or after a comma does not name a thing outright: in 'The sound was constant, a soft, vibrating drone' neither 'The sound' (a pointer) nor 'a soft, vibrating drone' (a description of it) is the label; go back to the sentence that names the sound ('the low, steady hum'). Do not go further than you must.

**Step 3. A pointer is never a label.** A pointer is one of these, and nothing else:
(a) a pronoun alone: it, this, that, they, them, he, she, here, there, one;
(b) any phrase that starts with this, that, these, those or such ('This smell', 'That familiar feeling', 'these signs', 'those simpler days');
(c) 'the', 'a' or 'an' plus one bare word from this list: sound, noise, smell, scent, odour, odor, aroma, fragrance, sight, feeling, sensation, memory, image, picture, thought, moment. 'The sound' is a pointer. 'The sharp sound' is not.
Use a pointer as the label, with `no_fuller_name` true, only when no noun anywhere in the passage names the thing. Never use it because the naming is far away or plain.

**Step 4. Holder words.** 'a vivid picture', 'a memory', 'an image', 'a thought' only announce a thing. Treat them as pointers. The naming is what the picture or the memory is of. It usually comes just after: go forward for it. Drop 'a memory of' and 'pictures of' from the front of a label.

**Step 5. Where a label starts and stops.**
- A thing (an object, a person, a place, a smell, a sound). Start at the first word of its naming phrase: the, a, his, its, a number or count word, or the first describing word. Keep the describing words in front of the noun. A name of the form 'X of Y' starts at X ('The rough texture of the tweed'). Keep one short phrase right after the noun that says what it is of or which one it is ('of ancient paper', 'from the microphone', 'in the percussion'). Stop before a verb, before a comma that adds description ('heavy with juice'), before which, that, who or where, and before 'near ...' or 'nearby'. If you are unsure where to stop, stop earlier: where a label stops is not compared.
- Never cut a naming phrase down to its bare noun: not 'scent' for 'Its lanolin scent', not 'girl', not 'pallets'. A plain re-naming that the passage itself writes ('the mess', 'the roses') is allowed when it is the naming in the evidence sentence.
- A scene or a happening (no noun of its own names it).
  (i) Something the Mind of this entry does or is: never put the Mind in the label. Leave off its name or pronoun, a role phrase set off by commas after the name, a part of its body that stands for it ('his hand', 'her feet'), helper words (had, has, was, were, would, is) and words ending in -ly in front of the doing word. Start at the doing word. If there is no doing word, start at the first word after the helper. 'Sam, an apprentice locksmith, automatically reached for the heavy toolbox' gives 'reached for the heavy toolbox'. 'She was a little girl again, watching her grandfather shave for Sunday church' gives 'a little girl again, watching her grandfather shave'.
  (ii) A word of noticing or recalling right after the Mind is a lead-in too: saw, had seen, watched, observed, heard, noticed, felt, pictured, remembered, recalled. Leave it off. The label is what was seen or recalled. 'He had seen countless pallets move down the conveyor belt' gives 'countless pallets move down the conveyor belt'.
  (iii) Something another person or thing does: start at that doer's naming. 'Judge Davies would strike her gavel twice'.
  (iv) Never label only the thing the action is done to: not 'the heavy toolbox', not 'the pool', not 'countless pallets'.
  Keep the doing word and what it is done to or where it goes. Stop before a tail that starts with for, when, while, as, before, after or because, and before a tail that only says when or how often ('decades ago', 'exactly at opening time', 'every day'). Stop at the end of the sentence.
- A length of time in front ('Years of', 'Decades of', 'Decades spent'): leave it off when two or more words are left that name what was lived ('daily milking', 'managing busy lunchtimes'). Keep the whole phrase when fewer are left ('Forty winters of roofing').
- Never more than 12 words. If the naming phrase is longer, stop after the 12th word.
- If you and another labeler would stop a word or two apart, that is harmless. Labels are compared by where they start in the passage, not letter by letter.

**Step 6. These are never the label.**
- For every Noetic: a length of time alone ('twenty years', 'his career', 'his fifty years'). A word that only counts or groups other things ('three main flaws', 'its parts', 'four distinct segments', 'these signs'). The how-much words or the rate words alone: those go in `measure`.
- For `^2` and `^3` only: the Mind's own pull or push named as a feeling ('a surge of satisfaction', 'a distinct aversion', 'a quiet yearning'), and what the Mind did in response ('she quickly turned away'). When the passage names what they are aimed at, label that. A feeling is the label only when the feeling is itself what the Mind is drawn to or repelled by.
- In the other Noetics a feeling or an action can be the thing. A remembered fear can be a `^9`. An action done every day can be the `^7` label (rule 6e).
All of these stay in the support.

**Step 7. Write the supporting quote (`support`).** Copy whole sentences, from the first word to the full stop. Copy the unbroken run from the sentence that holds your label to the evidence sentence. Most of the time that is one sentence. For an `^8`/`^9` pair, copy from the sentence of the `^8` label through the sentence of the `^9` label; both entries carry the same support. If your label is a plain re-naming ('the mess', 'The recording') or leans on an earlier naming with its, their, his or her ('Its simple presence'), and the sentence just before says what it is, start one sentence earlier. Add no other sentence. Never more than 4 sentences. Do not trim inside a sentence.

**Step 8. `measure` (only `^4` and `^7`).** Copy the shortest unbroken stretch that states how much (`^4`) or the rate and pattern (`^7`). It must lie inside the support. If the sentence states it in two places, copy the first place that lies outside your label. If the only place lies inside your label, copy that ('daily' in 'daily milking'). An 'every time ...' or 'whenever ...' clause is copied whole. It belongs to the measure, never to the label.

**Step 9. `mind` and `relative_to` are labels. Do not quote them afresh.**
- `mind`: the `label` of that Mind's `^1` entry, character for character. For a Mind the label is the name only, at its first full mention ('George', not 'George, the puppeteer').
- `relative_to` for `^8`: the `label` of its `^9`. For `^9`: the `label` of its `^8`. Character for character.
- `relative_to` for `^6`, the whole. Find it in this order.
  (a) Look in the sentence that holds the first part, before the part. Then go back one sentence at a time. Take the nearest naming, as that sentence words it ('The process', 'The recording', 'The problem'). Do not swap it for an earlier, different name.
  (b) Skip Minds, pointers, and phrases that only count or group the parts ('three main areas', 'its parts', 'Each element', 'several distinct phases').
  (c) A possessive counts as a naming: in 'the issue's constituent parts' the whole is 'the issue'. In 'the steps for X', 'the parts of X', 'the components of X' the whole is X, starting at X ('propagating her prize orchid', 'a hive inspection').
  (d) If a doing word stands between that naming and the parts, the sentence says something is done to the parts. It does not say the naming is made of them. 'The task involved dismantling the main pivot bolt, the spring mechanism, and the cage assembly.' Skip that naming and go back to the thing the doing is done to ('a complex derailleur'). When no doing word stands between ('The process involved several distinct phases. First, ...'; 'The problem involved three components: ...'), the naming is the whole.
  (e) Every part of one list carries the same whole.
- All other Noetics: `relative_to` is empty.

**Step 10. One thing, one entry.** For one Noetic and one Mind, a thing gets one entry however often the passage comes back to it. If the passage states the role twice, use the first statement: the first sentence that passes step 1 for that Noetic. Three exceptions.
(1) For `^4`, two different sizes for one thing are two entries (rule 10g).
(2) If one trigger brings two different things to Mind and the bringing words cover both, write two pairs. The `^8` entry is written twice with the same label. Each copy points at its own `^9`.
(3) If several noticed things bring one thing to Mind, write one pair per noticed thing. The `^9` entry is written once per trigger with the same label. Each copy points back at its own `^8`.
Exception 3 says how to write the entries. It does not say that such a pair is Cause and Effect. Rule 15 decides clear, uncertain or reasoning, as written.

**What the label names.**
- `^1`: the Mind. `support`: a sentence that holds the name.
- `^2`: the Idea the Mind has an affinity for and is attracted toward.
- `^3`: the Idea the Mind is adverse to and repelled by.
- `^4`: the Idea that resonates with the Mind. `measure`: the words that state how strongly or how weakly it impresses the Mind.
- `^5`: the Idea or Ideas the Mind is composed of (what it has lived, learned, come to believe, become skilled in).
- `^6`: the Idea that another Idea is composed of (one part). `relative_to`: the Idea they compose (the whole).
- `^7`: what the rate words count: the thing this Mind meets or does again and again. `measure`: the words that state the rate and pattern of exposure. (Where a cue and the Mind's response both come round each time, the entry keeps both: the cue in the measure, the response in the label. Which of the two Part A means by 'an Idea' the Mind 'is exposed to' is the owner's to say.)
- `^8`: the Idea that triggers a different Idea to come to Mind.
- `^9`: the Idea brought to Mind.

**Worked examples.** Every quote from a numbered passage below was checked by a small script as an exact copy (verify.py in my temp folder: 216 quotes, 0 not exact). Those passages are from the spent 428. They may be shown for teaching and are never scored again. The frozen guide must use made-up twins of them. W8, W9 and the second half of W6 are already made-up.

W1, the owner's 'girl' case (V388). 'Maria finished trimming Mr. Henderson's hair and applied a splash of aftershave. The clean, sharp scent instantly transported her. She was a little girl again, watching her grandfather shave for Sunday church. She remembered the warmth of his hand, the neat comb of his hair, and the gentle way he always smiled at her.'
Step 1: the bringing words are 'instantly transported her'. Step 2: the trigger is named in that sentence: 'The clean, sharp scent'. The thing brought to Mind is not named there, so look in the next sentence. It is a scene. Step 5(i): leave off the Mind and the helper word ('She was'); keep the doing word and what it is done to; stop before the tail 'for Sunday church'.
`^8`: mind 'Maria'; label 'The clean, sharp scent'; relative_to 'a little girl again, watching her grandfather shave'; support 'The clean, sharp scent instantly transported her. She was a little girl again, watching her grandfather shave for Sunday church.'
`^9`: mind 'Maria'; label 'a little girl again, watching her grandfather shave'; relative_to 'The clean, sharp scent'; the same support.
Wrong: label 'girl' (the remembered childhood scene is lost). Wrong: label 'her grandfather' (a person inside the scene, not the scene). 'for Sunday church' is not lost: it is in the support. No second `^9` for the last sentence: it adds detail to the same memory (rule 2). No `^7` for 'he always smiled at her': rate words inside a remembered scene (rule 6a).

W2, the owner's 'pallets' case (V237). 'Omar guided his forklift through the busy loading bay. He had seen countless pallets move down the conveyor belt, day in and day out. His hands and feet automatically adjusted the machine's position. He rarely needed to look directly at the incoming cargo anymore. His muscles simply knew where to place the forks to lift the next load.'
Step 1: the rate words sit in the second sentence, in two places ('countless', 'day in and day out'). Step 5(ii): leave off the lead-in 'He had seen'; start at the doer of the happening; stop before the tail that says how often. Step 8: 'countless' lies inside the label, so the measure is the next place.
`^7`: mind 'Omar'; label 'countless pallets move down the conveyor belt'; measure 'day in and day out'; support 'He had seen countless pallets move down the conveyor belt, day in and day out.'; certainty clear (the rate words pass rule 6a, and the passage says what the exposure did: 'automatically adjusted', 'rarely needed to look').
`^5`: mind 'Omar'; label 'where to place the forks'; support 'His muscles simply knew where to place the forks to lift the next load.' (a named skill, rule 6b: 'knew where to').
No `^5` on the pallets label from the labeler: the program adds the `^5` that goes with a clear `^7` (rule 6c).
Wrong: label 'pallets' or 'countless pallets' (the repeated activity of pallets moving down a conveyor is lost).

W3, a pointing-back phrase (V018, first three sentences). 'Chloe carefully unwrapped an old book. The dry, dusty scent of ancient paper filled the cool storeroom. This smell pulled her back to her university library's quiet stacks.'
Step 1: the bringing words are 'pulled her back to', in the third sentence. Step 2: the trigger in that sentence is 'This smell'. Step 3: it starts with 'This', so it is a pointer. Go back one sentence: 'The dry, dusty scent of ancient paper'. Step 5: keep the 'of' phrase; stop before the verb 'filled'.
`^8`: mind 'Chloe'; label 'The dry, dusty scent of ancient paper'; relative_to 'her university library's quiet stacks'; support 'The dry, dusty scent of ancient paper filled the cool storeroom. This smell pulled her back to her university library's quiet stacks.'
`^9`: label 'her university library's quiet stacks'; relative_to 'The dry, dusty scent of ancient paper'; the same support.
Wrong: label 'This smell' (a pointer; check C7 refuses it). Wrong: label 'an old book' (the passage says the scent did the bringing).

W4, the naming in the evidence sentence wins when it is not a pointer (V338 and V049).
V338: '... A sudden metallic clanging from the industrial dryer made her flinch. Then she spotted a pile of embroidered pillowcases, and she felt a sense of calm return. The dryer noise faded quickly in her awareness.'
`^4`: mind 'Martha'; label 'The dryer noise'; measure 'faded quickly in her awareness'; support 'The dryer noise faded quickly in her awareness.' Do not go back to 'A sudden metallic clanging from the industrial dryer': 'The dryer noise' is a naming, not a pointer. 'made her flinch' has no size word, so it gives no `^4` (rule 10e).
V049: 'A wrench slipped, hitting the metal frame with a distinct clang. The sharp sound made him pause, suddenly hearing a snare drum in his thoughts.'
`^8`: label 'The sharp sound'; relative_to 'a snare drum'. `^9`: label 'a snare drum'; relative_to 'The sharp sound'. Both carry the support 'The sharp sound made him pause, suddenly hearing a snare drum in his thoughts.' Not 'a distinct clang': the evidence sentence has its own naming.

W5, go back only when the evidence sentence does not name the thing; where a label stops (V014, first three sentences). 'Bernard unfolded a roll of raw tweed. Its lanolin scent filled the small shop, a rich, earthy woolliness. Instantly, he pictured his grandfather's old overcoat, heavy and warm, worn through countless winters.'
The arrival word is 'Instantly' with 'he pictured' (rule 2, test ii). The trigger is not named in that sentence, so go back one sentence and take the naming of what was noticed: 'Its lanolin scent'. Stop before the verb 'filled'.
`^8`: label 'Its lanolin scent'; relative_to 'his grandfather's old overcoat'. `^9`: label 'his grandfather's old overcoat' (stop at the comma); relative_to 'Its lanolin scent'. Support for both: 'Its lanolin scent filled the small shop, a rich, earthy woolliness. Instantly, he pictured his grandfather's old overcoat, heavy and warm, worn through countless winters.'
Wrong: 'Its lanolin scent filled the small shop' (runs past the name; harmless for the count, but not the rule). Wrong: 'a roll of raw tweed'.

W6, a breakdown and its whole (V238), and work done on a thing (made-up).
V238: 'Michael listened intently to the playback. The recording needed work. If the passage also gives what the kind lacks, the entry is clear. The list is closed: hold nothing else. These kinds wait on the owner. This rule does not say what any definition means.
- **H2-COMFORT (`^2`).** The passage says only that a thing gave the Mind a good feeling: comfort, warmth, calm, peace, relief, satisfaction, pleasure. No word of affinity is aimed at the thing (liked, loved, enjoyed, preferred, admired, appreciated, cherished, fond of). No pull is stated (drawn to, a pull toward, could not resist). No move toward it is shown (sought it out, lingered over it, went back to it, chose it). Example: 'Its simple presence offered a small sense of comfort.' - **H3-NOPULL (`^3`).** The passage says only that a thing did not draw the Mind or did not interest it: 'held little appeal', 'held no appeal', 'did not interest her', 'left him cold', 'without a second glance'. - **H3-BORED (`^3`).** The passage says only that a thing bored the Mind, or that the Mind found it dull, tedious or uninspiring. If the passage says both this and what H3-NOPULL describes, use H3-BORED. If a word of dislike is also there ('disliked them, finding them tedious'), the entry is a clear `^3`.
- **H5-ROLE (`^5`).** The passage gives a role or a life stage together with an experience word from this list: seasoned, veteran, experienced, long-time, lifelong, master, expert, old hand. It does not say what was lived or learned in it: 'the seasoned barber', 'a veteran locksmith'. The label is the role phrase with its experience word. Not held: a role with a length of time ('a fishmonger for nearly sixty years') is a clear `^5` under rule 6(b). Not written at all: a plain job title or life stage with no experience word and no length of time ('a taxi driver', 'the cobbler', 'a retired teacher', 'a young florist', 'as a student'). For those write no entry, no held entry and no note.
- **H7-RESULT (`^7`).** The passage shows only that the Mind now does a thing without thinking, automatically or by habit, and no words pass the rate test (rule 6a) for that thing. The label is the action. The `measure` is the without-thinking words. Example: 'Without thinking, he adjusted the ear defenders over his ears.' If words pass: clear when the effect on the Mind is stated, H7-NOEFFECT when it is not. 6. **`^5` is what the Mind is made of. `^7` is the rate and pattern of exposure.**
(a) **The rate test for `^7`.** These pass: (i) a schedule or frequency: every morning, each Tuesday and Friday, every day, daily, nightly, weekly, twice a week, every time ..., whenever ..., always, often, regularly, day in and day out, again and again, over and over; (ii) a count of repeats: countless, hundreds of times, thousands of times, time after time; (iii) a length of time joined by 'of' to a plural noun for something that comes round again: years of early mornings, sixty years of shows.
These do not pass. A length of time alone, or joined to a job, a place or an activity (thirty years on the wards, years of cutting hair, decades spent managing busy lunchtimes, years of loading and unloading): an -ing word after 'of' or 'spent' does not pass. A number of years, winters, seasons or decades: that is a length of time, not a count of repeats (forty winters, many isolated winters). Practising with no rate. One thing said or done once. Usual, familiar, everyday or routine standing alone. Words that only say the Mind acts without thinking (automatically, without thinking, instinctively). Words for exposure with no break (constant, steady: see H7-UNBROKEN).
The rate words must say how often this Mind meets or does the thing. Three cases give no `^7` entry and no held entry. One: rate words on something another person did, when the passage does not show this Mind meeting it each time. Two: rate words inside a remembered scene ('the gentle way he always smiled at her', 'where she often fell asleep'). Three: 'always', 'never', 'usually' or 'often' on what a thing does to the Mind when it is met ('always made her wince slightly', 'always brought back vivid pictures of her grandmother's old armchair'): that says the result is the same each time, not how often the Mind meets the thing.
(b) **`^5` needs a named thing the Mind has lived, learned, come to believe or become skilled in.** Label what was lived or learned, never the length of time alone: 'parcels burst open on the rollers', not 'her thirty years here'; 'every type of handwriting imaginable', not 'his career'. A standing skill or habit that the passage names as the Mind's own counts: 'a habit', 'second nature', 'ingrained', 'muscle memory', 'had learned to', 'knew how / where / what to'. Words that only say how an action is done now ('automatically', 'without thinking', 'effortlessly', 'precise and unhurried', 'familiar', 'no longer needed to look') name no such thing: write no `^5` for those words alone.
Which naming. If the evidence sentence names an experience and a habit or skill it left, label the experience. If the experience is only a length of time ('many isolated winters', 'thirty-five years'), label the habit or skill ('a familiar pattern'). If the sentence names two experiences, label the first ('worked in this canteen', not 'generations pass through').
Roles. A role with a length of time ('a fishmonger for nearly sixty years') is a clear `^5`; label the role with its length of time. A role with an experience word and no length of time is held under H5-ROLE. A plain job title or life stage with neither gives no `^5` entry and no held entry.
(c) **One statement that gives a rate and an experience** ('Years of daily milking had shaped every gesture'). Write the `^7` entry: label 'daily milking', measure 'daily'. Do not write a `^5` entry with the same label as your own `^7` entry, clear or held, for that Mind. spec.matching_algorithm_precise:
Plain Python. No model. No project code. Every constant is fixed in the plan before any new label exists. I ran a sketch of it, read-only: on the old labels (core.py, rows.py, reasons.py, cases.py, case_reasons.py) and on a hand-made fixture of made-up passages (fixture.py). The sketch is in my temp folder. It is not the frozen program. On the old labels it prints the same nine rows as the draft's sketch and as the reviewer's own copy.

STEP 0. CLEAN-UP. In the passage and in every quoted field: curly quotes become straight quotes; every run of white space becomes one space; ends are trimmed. All positions below are character positions in the cleaned passage.

STEP 1. WORDS. A word is every unbroken run of the characters A-Z, a-z, 0-9, lower-cased, with its start and end position. So 'grandfather's' is two words, 'grandfather' and 's'. A content word has 2 or more characters and is not one of the 34 filler words of tools/verdict.py (the, a, an, of, to, in, on, at, and, or, his, her, their, its, he, she, it, that, this, was, had, with, for, from, by, as, him, them, they, is, were, be, been, not).

STEP 2. SENTENCES. A sentence ends after a run of . ! or ? (plus any closing quote or bracket) that is followed by a space or the end of the text. Exception: a single full stop right after Mr, Mrs, Ms, Dr, St, Prof, Sr, Jr, No, vs, etc, e.g or i.e does not end a sentence. Semicolons do not end sentences. (On the 428 old passages this gives 1,885 sentences.)

STEP 3. LOCATE EVERY FIELD (after the checker has passed the entry). A quote 'occurs' at a place only if the character before it and the character after it are not a letter or a digit.
- support: the first place it occurs in the passage, widened to whole sentences.
- a `^1` label: the first place the name occurs in the passage, whatever the support.
- every other label: every place it occurs inside the widened support. These are its candidate places. Most labels have exactly one.
- measure: every place it occurs inside the widened support (candidate places).
- mind: the place of the label of that team's `^1` entry with the same string.
- relative_to for `^8` and `^9`: the candidate places of the partner entry's label (the checker has made sure the partner exists).
- relative_to for `^6`: the place where the whole occurs that ends nearest before the start of this entry's first label place; if there is none before it, the first place in the passage.
- a dropped entry has no places.
Why a `^1` label is located in the whole passage: a reviewer showed that two teams may copy two different sentences that both hold the name, and every entry of that Mind then failed with it. Why candidate places: rule 16 step 7 lets a support start one sentence earlier. If the label string also occurs in that earlier sentence, 'first place in the support' would put the two teams' labels at different places for no reason. Fixture passages F1 and F2 test both.

STEP 3b. THE ^5 THAT GOES WITH A ^7. If a team wrote a `^5` entry whose label is the same thing (step 5) as the label of one of its own `^7` entries, clear or held, for the same Mind, that `^5` entry is taken out of every row and counted as 'twin written by the labeler'. No re-ask. For every located clear `^7` entry (class '^7') the program makes one twin: a `^5` entry with the same Mind and the same label places. Twins are used only in the row '^5 with twins'.

STEP 4. WORD SETS. W(span) = the positions (0, 1, 2, ...) of the words that lie wholly inside the span. C(span) = the content words among them; if there are none, all of W(span).

STEP 5. THREE TESTS. For two single places p and q:
- SAME_THING(p, q): C(p) and C(q) share at least one word at the same position; and the first word of p and the first word of q are at most 2 word positions apart. In plain words: the two labels start at the same place, give or take two words, and overlap. Where they stop is free.
- OVERLAP(p, q): C(p) and C(q) share at least one word at the same position.
For two fields with candidate places, a test holds if it holds for at least one pair of their places.
- SAME_FIELD: both empty = yes. One empty and one filled = no. Otherwise SAME_THING.

STEP 6. THE CLASS OF AN ENTRY (exactly one).
- held: 'held ^n'. The hold code is compared after pairing.
- ambiguous with other_candidate 'reasoning': 'uncertain ^n' (rule 15(d)).
- ambiguous otherwise: 'ambiguous ^n'.
- clear `^9` with reached_by 'reasoning': '^9 reached by reasoning'.
- clear `^6` with clue true: '^6 clue'.
- every other clear entry: '^n'. Only this class counts toward a bar. I call it the bar row.
A dropped entry with a valid noetic and certainty gets its class the same way from its own valid fields.

STEP 7. THE SAME READING. Entry x of team A and entry y of team B are the same reading when they are in the same passage and the same class, both are located, and all of these hold:
R1. SAME_THING(x.label, y.label).
R2. SAME_FIELD(x.mind, y.mind). Skipped for `^1` and `^6`.
R3. SAME_FIELD(x.relative_to, y.relative_to). Only for `^6`, `^8`, `^9`.
R4. Only for `^4` and `^7`: OVERLAP(x.measure, y.measure).
The supports are never compared. A support still matters in one way: it says in which sentences a label is looked for. Two teams that rest the same words on sentences that do not overlap are not matched ('the tweed' in an earlier sentence against 'the tweed' in a later one, V134). That is meant: rule 16 step 1 tells both teams which sentence is the evidence sentence. (The draft said 'a long or a short support cannot change a score'. A reviewer showed that was false. It is withdrawn.)

STEP 8. ONE-TO-ONE PAIRING, per passage and per class, over located entries.
1. Order team A's entries by (start of first label place, end of first label place, position in the file). Order team B's the same way.
2. For each A entry list the B entries that are the same reading. Sort that list by: smaller difference between the two first label starts first; then more shared content words in the labels; then B order.
3. Find the largest possible set of pairs with the standard augmenting-path method (Kuhn's algorithm): take the A entries in order; give each its first free candidate; if that candidate is taken, try to move the A entry that holds it to its next candidate, and so on. Each entry is used at most once.
The NUMBER of pairs is the largest possible, so it does not depend on the order. The order only decides which leftover entry gets which reason. With the fixed orders the result is the same on every run. The checker refuses duplicates (C8); if one still slips through, the scorer keeps the first and counts the other as a duplicate.

STEP 9. COUNTS per class over all analysed passages. A = team A's entries in the class: located ones plus dropped ones that stay in the row. B the same for team B. M = pairs. only A = A - M. only B = B - M.

STEP 10. ONE REASON FOR EVERY UNMATCHED BAR-ROW ENTRY x. The first that applies. Reasons describe. They never change a count.
0. DROPPED: x is a dropped entry.
1. STATUS: the other team has a located entry of the same Noetic in a DIFFERENT class that passes R1 and R2 (the same thing written as held, ambiguous, uncertain, clue or reasoning).
2. FIELD: the other team has an unmatched entry of the same class that passes R1 and R2 and fails R3 or R4. The failed test is recorded.
3. MIND: the other team has an unmatched entry of the same class that passes R1 and fails R2.
4. START: the other team has an unmatched entry of the same class that passes R2, fails R1, rests on the same evidence, and whose label OVERLAPs x's label. In plain words: the same words, but the two labels start more than 2 words apart.
5. OTHER_LABEL: as 4, but the two labels share no word at the same place. In plain words: the same evidence, another label.
   'The same evidence' means: R3 passes (`^6`, `^8`, `^9`); or R4 passes (`^4`, `^7`); or the two supports share a sentence (`^2`, `^3`, `^5`).
6. OTHER_NOETIC: the other team pointed at the same words under another Noetic (not `^1`), in an entry that is clear or held, for the same Mind. For `^4` and `^7`: an entry whose label or measure passes OVERLAP with x's measure. For the others: an entry whose label passes SAME_THING with x's label, or whose measure passes OVERLAP with x's label. The other Noetic is recorded.
7. FACES_A_DROP: none of the above, and the other team's only entries of this class in the passage are dropped ones.
8. OTHER_THING: none of the above, and the other team has at least one located bar-row entry of this Noetic in the passage.
9. ABSENT: the other team has no bar-row entry of this Noetic in the passage.
Read them this way. FIELD and START are pointing misses. OTHER_LABEL is a pointing miss for `^6`, `^8` and `^9`, where the same whole or the same partner ties the two entries together. For `^2`, `^3`, `^4`, `^5` and `^7` OTHER_LABEL is NOT called pointing: the two teams may have picked different things, and some of those picks turn on questions that are the owner's (the excavator or its might; the experience or the trait). STATUS, OTHER_THING and ABSENT are about whether the role is there. OTHER_NOETIC is a role mix-up. DROPPED and FACES_A_DROP are format.

STEP 11. POINTING PAIRS AND THE CEILING. After step 8, pair the leftover bar-row entries of the two teams one to one, again with the largest-set method. Two leftovers may pair if their relation is FIELD or START; for `^6`, `^8` and `^9` also OTHER_LABEL. P = the number of such pairs. Pointing ceiling = (M + P) / (M + only A + only B - P). The same line is printed a second time with OTHER_LABEL allowed for every Noetic, marked 'not all of this is pointing'. Neither line counts toward a bar. (The draft counted pointing misses per entry and took the smaller team total, so two entries could lean on one partner. A reviewer showed that this put `^9` at 0.847 when one-to-one pairing gives 0.797.)

CHOICES KEPT FROM THE DRAFT, AND WHY.
- The label test: overlap AND a start at most 2 words apart. It forgives where a label stops, which is what the owner described ('Its lanolin scent' against 'Its lanolin scent filled the small shop'). It does not forgive a different thing inside the same stretch: 'her grandfather' inside the remembered scene; 'its mechanical might' against 'the heavy excavator'.
- It gives old labels no lift. MEASURED on the old labels (old `words` standing in for the label): entry agreement at start tolerance 0, at 2, and with no start rule is ^2 0.526 / 0.559 / 0.629; ^5 0.388 / 0.447 / 0.563; ^6 0.308 / 0.381 / 0.402; ^7 0.227 / 0.296 / 0.328; ^8 0.456 / 0.472 / 0.541; ^9 0.430 / 0.478 / 0.529. So any gain in a new attempt has to come from the teams following rule 16, not from the scorer. The tolerance of 2 is fixed before labels; both other values are always reported.
- The measure test for `^4` and `^7` is OVERLAP, not 'same sentence'. One sentence can hold two sizes for one thing (rule 10g). The sketch now uses the same test as this text; a reviewer found the draft's sketch used 'same sentence' in one place.
- No second tier in the pairing. Pointing misses are shown by the reasons and the ceiling line. They never count toward a bar.
- Words are split at the apostrophe, so a label that ends at a possessive stem ('Mr. Henderson' inside 'Mr. Henderson's hair') keeps its last word.
A reviewer stress-tested the test on the old labels: team B labels stretched to 10 words changed 1 match in 9 rows; labels started 2 words early and stretched gave no real lift; a team that writes a second hedge entry scores 0.5 on that item.

WHAT IT DOES ON KNOWN CASES (old labels mapped to the new fields; cases.py and case_reasons.py).
- V014, 'Its lanolin scent' against 'Its lanolin scent filled the small shop': same start, overlap. `^8` matched 1, `^9` matched 1.
- V388, 'a little girl again, watching her grandfather shave for Sunday church' against 'She was a little girl again': the starts are 2 words apart. Matched.
- V237, `^7`: 'countless pallets' against 'pallets move down the conveyor belt', both with the measure 'day in and day out': starts 1 word apart. Matched.
- V099, `^3`: 'shriveled, diseased berries' against 'some shriveled, diseased berries hung limp and unappealing'. Matched (it missed under v1.2).
- V018: 'The dry, dusty scent of ancient paper' against 'This smell'. No overlap. `^8`: only A 1, only B 1, reason OTHER_LABEL (the same Effect ties them). `^9`: the Effects are the same but their triggers differ: only A 1, only B 1, reason FIELD. The program cannot know 'This smell' is the scent. Only rule 16 and check C7 fix it.
- V200, `^2`: 'the heavy excavator' against 'its mechanical might'. Only A 1, only B 1, reason OTHER_LABEL. Not counted as agreement, and for `^2` not counted as pointing.
- V338, `^4`: team A has 1 entry, team B has 2. Matched 0, only A 1, only B 2. Reasons: FIELD, FIELD, OTHER_LABEL.
- V238, `^6`: the four parts sit at the same places; the wholes 'the playback' and 'The recording' do not. Matched 0, only A 4, only B 4, all FIELD.
- V291, V158, V002 (the reviewer's cases): 'automatically reached for the heavy toolbox' against 'the heavy toolbox', 'Judge Davies would strike her gavel twice' against 'strike her gavel twice', 'Tom arrived at the pool' against 'the pool': each 3 words apart, no match. That is why rule 16 step 5 now fixes where a happening label starts.

KNOWN LIMITS. (1) The test cannot tell 'the same thing under another name' from 'a different thing in the same stretch'. That is why such pairs never count. (2) It is start-anchored, so a lead-in of three or more words kept by one team breaks a match; rule 16 step 5 says which lead-ins to leave off. (3) Exact copies are case-sensitive. (4) The sentence splitter is a fixed rule, not a parser; a new abbreviation would split a sentence for both teams alike. (5) With candidate places, two identical strings inside one support are treated as one thing. That is rare, and the support is capped at 4 sentences.
spec.measures_and_bars:
EVERY BAR, THE HOLD TABLE, THE OUTCOME WORDS, THE SEAL CONDITIONS AND THE NINE CONVENTIONS ARE PROPOSALS. They take effect only when the owner signs them, before any new passage is sealed. Nothing changes after labels are seen. I do not set them.

KEPT FROM PLAN v1.2. Only cases count, never passages where neither team marked the Noetic. Only clear entries count toward a bar. Uncertain pairs (rule 15(d)) and conclusions reached by reasoning (rule 15(b)) are reported apart, with no bar. The Mind and the related thing must agree. At least 50 cases and at least 50 absences, or no verdict. A program computes every number and every outcome word. No guide change, no relabeling, no dropped passage and no changed bar after labels are seen. A new attempt needs new passages and a new plan version. The verdict is invalid if more than 5% of passages could not be labeled by a team after three tries, or more than 5% of a team's entries are dropped.

THE COUNTS, per Noetic `^1` to `^9`, over ENTRIES of the bar row (clear entries; not a `^9` reached by reasoning; not a `^6` clue).
A = team A's entries. B = team B's entries. Both include dropped entries that stay in the row. M = entries both teams gave, paired one to one (matching algorithm).
only A = A - M. These are extra for team A and missing from team B.
only B = B - M. These are extra for team B and missing from team A.
There is no answer key, so 'extra for one team' and 'missing from the other' are the same entries. Each is printed once.

PRIMARY MEASURE: entry agreement E = M / (M + only A + only B). In plain words: of every role either team wrote down, the share both wrote down, for the same Mind, pointing at the same place. One matching pair no longer covers for other unmatched entries in the same passage.
Always printed beside it: team A's share matched = M / A; team B's share matched = M / B; and fully matched cases = cases where no bar-row entry of either team is left over.

PRESENCE MEASURE (unchanged): Cohen's kappa on 'this passage has at least one bar-row entry for the Noetic', over all analysed passages.

MINIMUM COUNTS (unchanged). A case is a passage where at least one team gave a bar-row entry. At least 50 cases, and at least 50 passages where neither team gave one.

THE `^5` BAR ROW. The bar is on `^5` as the labelers wrote it, without the entries the program adds for each clear `^7`. The row '^5 with twins' is printed beside it with no bar. PROPOSED BARS. E at least 0.80. Kappa at least 0.60.
Why E. E is the entry-by-entry twin of the old measure. Keeping 0.80 on E keeps the bar from getting easier while the count gets stricter. E at 0.80 also forces both teams' shares to 0.80 or more. The easier choice is 0.80 on each team's own share (M / A and M / B), which lets E fall to 0.667. The owner sets the number.
Kappa is kept because the reviewed plan has it. It is a weak gate here: `^4` passes it at 0.677 while its entry agreement is 0.378. Nobody should read a kappa pass as agreement on presence.
What to expect, so that the number is chosen knowingly (ESTIMATE from reading, not a measurement; the feasibility reviewer and I agree on it): `^1` likely passes, not by much. `^8` and `^9` are about even, leaning under. `^2` and `^3` under. `^5`, `^6`, `^4` and `^7` fail. OUTCOME WORDS, computed by the program in this order.
1. NOT_ENOUGH_CASES: fewer than 50 cases or fewer than 50 absences.
2. NOT_LABELABLE_UNDER_THIS_METHOD: E below 0.80 or kappa below 0.60.
3. NO_VERDICT_WAITING_ON_OWNER (new word, my proposal): both bars are met, but more entries of this Noetic sit OUTSIDE the bar row than inside it. Outside = every entry of that Noetic in the held rows, the uncertain row, the ambiguous row, the row '^9 reached by reasoning' and the row '^6 clue', counted as matched + only A + only B in each. Inside = M + only A + only B of the bar row. This rule can only take a pass away. It can never turn a failure into anything else.
4. LABELABLE_UNDER_THIS_METHOD: otherwise. The line must print its scope: 'clear entries only; N entries held under codes ...; N clue entries; N uncertain entries; N reached by reasoning; N ambiguous; N dropped; not covered'.
5. Every other row: REPORTED_ONLY_NO_BAR.
The outcome uses the measured values. A failed bar is a failure. There is no 'pass with notes'.

INTERVALS. Entries inside one passage are not independent. KINDS (plain descriptions given to the writer).
K1, something noticed brings a quite different thing into a person's thoughts: 140.
K2a, a person is drawn toward one thing and put off by another: 120.
K2b, something lands strongly on a person, and something else hardly at all: 80.
K3, what a person has lived or learned over years shapes how they take something now: 60.
K4, someone takes a thing apart into named pieces: 70.
K5, the same thing over and over on a schedule has changed how a person acts: 100.
K6, an experienced person notices a small sign and knows what it means: 30 (rule 15 rows, no bar).
K7, a person works through clues step by step to a conclusion: 30 (rule 15(b) rows, no bar).
K8, purely physical description, no person's thoughts: 80.
K9, a person does ordinary things; nothing of likes, memories or habits is shown: 20.
K10, free: a person at work in the setting; the writer chooses what happens: 30.
Total 760. Each of `^2` to `^9` is asked for in at most 140 of the 760, so 50 absences are safe.

WHY THESE CHOICES.
- Change after review: K1 goes from 70 to 140 and K2a from 80 to 120. A reviewer showed that for the rows expected near 0.80 the outcome word would be decided mostly by which passages happened to be written. More K1 also keeps the bar rows of `^8` and `^9` larger than their uncertain rows, which the wider withheld-pass rule now needs. The cost is small: a free writer and a few cents of labeling. The price: the new set has a different mix from the first one, so the two attempts are even less comparable.
- The briefs are not tuned toward the new rules. That would make the test easy. K1 and K3 to K9 keep their wording from plan v1.2.
- K2 is split in two. The old K2 brief asked for three things in one passage. The two new briefs are its two halves, word for word.
- K5 at 100 and K2a at 120 guard `^7` and `^3`, whose bar rows shrink when held kinds are taken out. If a bar row still has fewer than 50 cases, the outcome is NOT_ENOUGH_CASES. It is not repaired afterwards.
- K8 goes from 60 to 80. `^1` had exactly 55 passages where neither team marked a Mind. That is close to the floor of 50.
- K10 keeps the test from being only stock phrasing. Roles that turn up unasked were the worst cases last time.

MECHANICAL CHECKS ONLY BEFORE SEALING (as before): drop a passage that contains a forbidden word, has fewer than 30 or more than 120 words, or repeats another exactly. Count the drops. Nobody reads the passages to choose among them. Then new ids, a fixed-seed shuffle, and the file hash in a new SEAL file, before any label team starts.

LABEL TEAMS, unchanged, for comparability. Team A: Claude (Sonnet) sub-agents, about 50 passages each (about 15 sub-agents for the verdict set, 3 for the practice pass), working apart. Team B: DeepSeek `deepseek-chat`, one passage per call, temperature 0. Both get guide v2.0 and the same checker, with up to three tries per passage.
